ev.amr_h_ixtlilxochitl.title: The ruler is slain
ev.amr_h_ixtlilxochitl.text: The Tepanecs of Azcapotzalco have attacked Texcoco. The ruler Ixtlilxochitl was killed before everyone's eyes, and his young son Nezahualcoyotl fled. The city has been handed over to Tepanec rule, and tribute now goes to them.
ev.amr_h_ixtlilxochitl.note: In 1418 the Tepanec ruler Tezozomoc crushed Texcoco; Ixtlilxochitl I was killed, and Nezahualcoyotl, by tradition, watched his death from hiding and spent years as a fugitive.
ev.amr_h_ixtlilxochitl.hide.success: The fugitives got away to the hills. You kept the secret.
ev.amr_h_ixtlilxochitl.hide.failure: The Tepanecs found out and wrecked your house.
ev.amr_h_tepanec_war.title: War with Azcapotzalco
ev.amr_h_tepanec_war.text: The Tepanec lord Maxtla demands submission and tribute. In Tenochtitlan people argue: bow down or fight. Itzcoatl and his counsellor Tlacaelel call for war, together with the exiled prince of Texcoco, Nezahualcoyotl.
ev.amr_h_tepanec_war.note: In 1428 Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan defeated the Tepanecs of Azcapotzalco, to whom they had paid tribute. The victory opened the way to the Mexica empire.
ev.amr_h_tepanec_war.fight.success: Azcapotzalco has fallen. The victors share out the Tepanec lands, and you got something too.
ev.amr_h_tepanec_war.fight.failure: Victory was won, but it cost you blood and goods.
ev.amr_h_triple_alliance.title: The Triple Alliance
ev.amr_h_triple_alliance.text: Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan have formed an alliance to share spoils and tribute and fight together. Itzcoatl ordered the old books burned: now the Mexica rewrite their history as a people chosen by the Sun.
ev.amr_h_triple_alliance.note: The Triple Alliance (1428) became the basis of the "Aztec Empire". According to accounts recorded by Sahagún, Itzcoatl ordered the old painted books destroyed because they were inconvenient for the new rulers.
ev.amr_h_nezahualcoyotl.title: Nezahualcoyotl returns
ev.amr_h_nezahualcoyotl.text: After many years in exile Nezahualcoyotl, the "Fasting Coyote", has returned and become ruler of Texcoco. He promises new laws, courts, schools, and gardens never seen before.
ev.amr_h_nezahualcoyotl.note: Nezahualcoyotl (1402–1472) ruled Texcoco from 1431. He was famous as a lawgiver, builder and poet; many poems recorded after the conquest are attributed to him.
ev.amr_h_moctezuma_i.title: Moctezuma the Elder
ev.amr_h_moctezuma_i.text: Moctezuma Ilhuicamina, the "Angry Lord who shoots at the sky", has been chosen as the new ruler. They say he will lead the armies further than anyone before him.
ev.amr_h_moctezuma_i.note: Moctezuma I ruled from 1440 to 1469. Under him the empire expanded to the Gulf coast, and an aqueduct and a dike were built in Tenochtitlan.
ev.amr_h_flood_1449.title: Flood and dike
ev.amr_h_flood_1449.text: The lake has risen and flooded Tenochtitlan. On Nezahualcoyotl's advice thousands of people are building a dike across the lake to separate fresh water from salt. Hands are needed.
ev.amr_h_flood_1449.note: After the flood of 1449, under Nezahualcoyotl's direction, a dike some 16 km long was built to separate the western part of the lake, with the city, from the salty waters.
ev.amr_h_famine.title: The famine of 1 Rabbit
ev.amr_h_famine.text: For the third year running frost and drought have killed the maize. The ruler hands out the stores, but they are not enough. People sell themselves and their children into slavery to the Totonacs on the coast for a few baskets of grain.
ev.amr_h_famine.note: The great famine of 1450–1454 was remembered by the year "1 Rabbit" (1454). Chronicles tell how many went to the coast and sold themselves into slavery to survive.
ev.amr_h_famine.share: Share your last food with the neighbours
ev.amr_h_famine.hoard: Keep your stores for your own
ev.amr_h_famine.coast: Go to the coast for grain
ev.amr_h_famine.coast.success: You came back with a sack of maize. It saved the household.
ev.amr_h_famine.coast.failure: The road wore you out, and you never got any grain.
ev.amr_h_new_fire_1455.title: The New Fire
ev.amr_h_new_fire_1455.text: An age of 52 years has ended. Across the valley fires are put out, old pots smashed, and people wait in the dark: will the sun rise again? At midnight on the hill of Huixachtlan the priests kindle a new fire, and runners carry it to every town.
ev.amr_h_new_fire_1455.note: The New Fire ceremony was held once every 52 years, when the beginnings of two calendar cycles coincided. It was held, among other years, in 1455 and 1507.
ev.amr_h_flower_wars.title: The "flower war"
ev.amr_h_flower_wars.text: The Alliance has agreed with Tlaxcala and Huexotzinco on wars by arrangement: on an appointed day the armies meet to take captives for the gods. The ward is sending its young men.
ev.amr_h_flower_wars.note: The "flower wars" (xochiyaoyotl) were ritual battles between the Alliance and the cities of the Puebla valley. Their aims were captives for sacrifice and military training; historians explain their origins differently.
ev.amr_h_flower_wars.go.success: You came back whole and honoured.
ev.amr_h_aqueduct.title: Water from Chapultepec
ev.amr_h_aqueduct.text: The stone aqueduct from the hill of Chapultepec is finished: fresh spring water now flows straight into the city. The water-carriers grumble and the housewives rejoice.
ev.amr_h_aqueduct.note: The Chapultepec aqueduct was built under Moctezuma I (around 1466). A double channel allowed one pipe to be cleaned while water flowed through the other.
ev.amr_h_nezahualcoyotl_death.title: The death of the poet
ev.amr_h_nezahualcoyotl_death.text: Nezahualcoyotl has died. Texcoco is in mourning. His young son Nezahualpilli has become ruler; they say he is learned in the stars and divination.
ev.amr_h_nezahualcoyotl_death.note: Nezahualcoyotl died in 1472. His son Nezahualpilli ruled until 1515 and was also famous for wisdom and strict laws.
ev.amr_h_tlatelolco.title: Tlatelolco conquered
ev.amr_h_tlatelolco.text: The ruler Axayacatl has gone to war against the neighbouring twin city of Tlatelolco. Its ruler is dead, and the great market now answers to Tenochtitlan.
ev.amr_h_tlatelolco.note: In 1473 Axayacatl annexed Tlatelolco, home of the largest market in Mesoamerica. Its ruler Moquihuix was killed.
ev.amr_h_tlatelolco.buy: Buy market stalls while they are cheap
ev.amr_h_tlatelolco.buy.success: A good deal: your stall at the market brings in income.
ev.amr_h_tlatelolco.buy.failure: The new overseers took the stall for themselves.
ev.amr_h_tarascan.title: Defeat in the west
ev.amr_h_tarascan.text: Axayacatl's army, sent against the Purépecha (Tarascans), has been routed. Only a small part came back. The wards mourn their dead, and for the first time people say the Alliance is not all-powerful.
ev.amr_h_tarascan.note: Around 1478–1479 Axayacatl's army suffered a heavy defeat by the Tarascans (Purépecha). The Tarascan frontier remained impregnable until the Spaniards came.
ev.amr_h_templo_mayor.title: The Great Temple dedicated
ev.amr_h_templo_mayor.text: The ruler Ahuitzotl has finished rebuilding the Great Temple. Rulers from all over the land, even enemies, were summoned to the dedication. The festivities lasted many days, and the blood of many captives was shed.
ev.amr_h_templo_mayor.note: The dedication of a rebuilt Templo Mayor in 1487 was accompanied by mass sacrifice of captives. The numbers given in the sources vary widely and are probably exaggerated.
ev.amr_h_ahuitzotl_flood.title: The waters of Acuecuexco
ev.amr_h_ahuitzotl_flood.text: Ahuitzotl ordered the water of a new spring brought into the city. But the spring proved too strong: the water flooded houses and chinampas, and the ruler himself, they say, was hurt fleeing the flood.
ev.amr_h_ahuitzotl_flood.note: Around 1499–1500 a new aqueduct from the Acuecuexco spring caused a flood in Tenochtitlan. According to some sources Ahuitzotl was injured then and later died of it.
ev.amr_h_moctezuma_ii.title: Moctezuma the Younger
ev.amr_h_moctezuma_ii.text: Moctezuma Xocoyotzin, stern and pious, has been chosen ruler. He dismissed commoner servants from the palace: now only nobles may serve him.
ev.amr_h_moctezuma_ii.note: Moctezuma II ruled from 1502. He sharpened the division between nobles and commoners at court and continued conquests until the Spaniards arrived.
ev.amr_h_new_fire_1507.title: The last New Fire
ev.amr_h_new_fire_1507.text: Another 52-year age has ended. In the dark everyone waits to see whether the fire will catch on the hill. It flared up, and the sun, say the priests, will live another age.
ev.amr_h_new_fire_1507.note: The 1507 ceremony turned out to be the last: the next, due in 1559, never took place, as by then the country had been conquered by the Spaniards.
ev.amr_h_new_fire_1507.renew: Smash the old pots and renew the house
ev.amr_h_omens.title: Omens
ev.amr_h_omens.text: At night a column of fire is seen in the east, a temple burned down by itself, and the lake boiled with no wind. People whisper that Moctezuma does not sleep and consults his diviners.
ev.amr_h_omens.note: The stories of eight omens before the Spaniards came were written down after the conquest and probably took shape largely in hindsight.
ev.amr_h_cortes.title: The strangers
ev.amr_h_cortes.text: Bearded men in shining armour have come from the sea, riding huge hornless deer, with thunder tubes that spit fire. Thousands of Tlaxcalans march with them. Moctezuma receives them in the city as guests.
ev.amr_h_cortes.note: Hernán Cortés landed on the coast in 1519, made an alliance with Tlaxcala and entered Tenochtitlan on 8 November 1519. Horses and firearms had never been seen here before.
ev.amr_h_noche_triste.title: The night of flight
ev.amr_h_noche_triste.text: The Spaniards attacked unarmed people at a festival in the temple courtyard, and the city rose. Moctezuma is dead. At night the strangers flee along the causeway, loaded with gold, pursued by warriors in canoes.
ev.amr_h_noche_triste.note: In May 1520 Pedro de Alvarado's men massacred people at the Toxcatl festival. On the night of 30 June – 1 July 1520 the Spaniards fled the city with heavy losses (the "Noche Triste").
ev.amr_h_noche_triste.fight.success: The enemy fled. You came back a hero of the ward.
ev.amr_h_noche_triste.fight.failure: In the dark and the crush you were wounded.
ev.amr_h_smallpox_mx.title: The great rash
ev.amr_h_smallpox_mx.text: An unknown disease came with the strangers: fever and pustules all over the body. People lie in their houses unable to rise, and there is no one to bring them water. The new ruler Cuitlahuac has died too.
ev.amr_h_smallpox_mx.note: The smallpox epidemic of 1520 killed a huge part of Mexico's population, including the ruler Cuitlahuac. The local people had no immunity to Old World diseases.
ev.amr_h_smallpox_mx.care.failure: You caught it and hovered between life and death for a long time.
ev.amr_h_smallpox_mx.isolate.success: The disease passed your house by.
ev.amr_h_fall.title: The fall of Tenochtitlan
ev.amr_h_fall.text: The strangers have returned with brigantines on the lake and tens of thousands of allies. The city is under siege: the causeways cut, the aqueduct destroyed, no water and no food. Cuauhtemoc will not surrender. Ward by ward the city is turning to ruins.
ev.amr_h_fall.note: The siege of Tenochtitlan lasted from May to 13 August 1521 and ended with the capture of Cuauhtemoc. The city was almost completely destroyed; the Spaniards built Mexico City on its site.
ev.amr_h_fall.defend.success: You survived the last battles. The city fell, but you are alive.
ev.amr_h_fall.defend.failure: You fell in the last battles for the city.
ev.amr_h_fall.flee: Flee across the lake with your family
ev.amr_h_fall.flee.success: At night you slipped past the brigantines and found shelter with kin on the shore.
ev.amr_h_fall.flee.failure: The canoe was spotted. You escaped empty-handed and lost everything.
ev.amr_h_new_spain.title: New masters
ev.amr_h_new_spain.text: Now tribute is collected for the Spaniards. Each town has been "entrusted" to some Spanish encomendero: people bring him cloaks, maize and labour. Churches are being built on the ruins of temples from the same stones.
ev.amr_h_new_spain.note: After 1521 the Spaniards introduced the encomienda: native towns were granted to conquistadors, who received tribute and labour in return for the duty to "convert" the inhabitants.
ev.amr_h_franciscans.title: The twelve friars
ev.amr_h_franciscans.text: Twelve friars in brown habits have walked barefoot into the city. Cortés knelt before them in front of everyone. The nobles watch, baffled: who can these men be, if the conqueror himself bows to them?
ev.amr_h_franciscans.note: In 1524 the "twelve apostles", Franciscans led by Martín de Valencia, arrived in Mexico City. They began mass baptisms and opened schools for noble children.
ev.amr_h_cuauhtemoc.title: The death of Cuauhtemoc
ev.amr_h_cuauhtemoc.text: News has come that Cortés took the captive Cuauhtemoc with him on a long expedition south, and there executed him on suspicion of conspiracy. The last ruler is gone.
ev.amr_h_cuauhtemoc.note: Cuauhtemoc was executed in 1525 during Cortés's expedition to Honduras.
ev.amr_h_viceroy.title: The viceroy
ev.amr_h_viceroy.text: A deputy of the Spanish king, a viceroy, has arrived from across the sea. They say he will also hear the complaints of the Indians. In Tlatelolco a college has opened where noble youths are taught Latin.
ev.amr_h_viceroy.note: Antonio de Mendoza, the first viceroy of New Spain, arrived in 1535. In 1536 the College of Santa Cruz at Tlatelolco opened for the sons of the native nobility.
ev.amr_h_viceroy.petition: File a complaint against the encomendero
ev.amr_h_viceroy.petition.success: The complaint was accepted and the tribute reduced a little.
ev.amr_h_viceroy.petition.failure: The encomendero found out about the complaint and took revenge.
ev.amr_h_cocoliztli.title: Cocoliztli
ev.amr_h_cocoliztli.text: A new plague: fever, bleeding from the nose, people burn up in a few days. The friars bury the dead in great pits. They say one in two is dying.
ev.amr_h_cocoliztli.note: The "cocoliztli" epidemic of 1545–1548 was one of the deadliest in Mexican history. Its nature is still debated.
ev.amr_h_cocoliztli.care.failure: You fell ill and survived by a miracle.
ev.amr_h_chanka.title: The Chanka at the gates
ev.amr_h_chanka.text: The warlike Chanka are marching on Cusco. The old Inca Viracocha has fled the city with his heir. A younger son, Cusi Yupanqui, has stayed, and he calls on everyone to defend the capital.
ev.amr_h_chanka.note: According to Inca tradition, in 1438 Cusi Yupanqui beat off the Chanka attack and became Inca under the name Pachacuti, "he who overturns the world". The date is conventional and based on chronicles.
ev.amr_h_chanka.defend.success: The Chanka were thrown back. They say the very stones of the field rose up as warriors to help Cusi Yupanqui.
ev.amr_h_chanka.defend.failure: Victory came at a high price: you were badly wounded.
ev.amr_h_cusco_rebuilt.title: A new Cusco
ev.amr_h_cusco_rebuilt.text: Pachacuti is rebuilding the capital: rivers are channelled in stone, the Sun temple of Coricancha is sheathed in gold sheets, and the city itself, they say, follows the outline of a puma. Thousands of people have been brought in to build.
ev.amr_h_cusco_rebuilt.note: Pachacuti (ruled c. 1438–1471) rebuilt Cusco to a single plan. The image of the puma-shaped city comes from the chronicles; how literally to take it is debated.
ev.amr_h_cusco_rebuilt.work.success: You learned to fit stones so closely that not even a needle can pass between them.
ev.amr_h_cusco_rebuilt.work.failure: A block slipped off its rollers. You survived, but were injured.
ev.amr_h_sacsayhuaman.title: The walls of Sacsayhuaman
ev.amr_h_sacsayhuaman.text: Gigantic zigzag walls are rising above the city: stones bigger than a house are dragged by thousands of mit'a workers. Your ayllu has sent its people for another term.
ev.amr_h_sacsayhuaman.note: The Sacsayhuaman complex was built over several decades, starting under Pachacuti. The stones in its walls weigh tens and hundreds of tonnes.
ev.amr_h_topa_north.title: Topa Inca's campaigns
ev.amr_h_topa_north.text: The young general Topa Inca Yupanqui is leading the armies north, to lands Cusco knew only by rumour. The ayllu is required to send warriors and porters.
ev.amr_h_topa_north.note: In the 1460s Topa Inca, son of Pachacuti, conquered lands as far as present-day Ecuador, including the Quito region, and then crushed the kingdom of Chimor on the coast.
ev.amr_h_topa_north.go.success: You came back with a reward: cloth from the royal storehouses.
ev.amr_h_topa_north.go.failure: You came back from the campaign sick and wasted.
ev.amr_h_quito_conquered.title: The Incas have come
ev.amr_h_quito_conquered.text: An Inca army has come from the south. The local lords resisted, but one by one the valleys bow before Topa Inca. Now there will be storehouses, roads, khipu keepers here, and settlers from the south.
ev.amr_h_quito_conquered.note: The Quito region entered the Inca realm in the 1460s under Topa Inca; it was finally subdued by Huayna Capac, who made Quito his northern residence.
ev.amr_h_quito_conquered.resist.success: You survived in the mountains and came back when things had calmed down.
ev.amr_h_quito_conquered.resist.failure: The lords were defeated. You were made a yana and driven south.
ev.amr_h_chimor.title: Craftsmen from Chan Chan
ev.amr_h_chimor.text: The coastal kingdom of Chimor has fallen. Its goldsmiths and weavers have been brought to Cusco with their families. Their work is finer than anything seen here.
ev.amr_h_chimor.note: Around 1470 the Incas conquered the kingdom of Chimor and its capital Chan Chan. Many of its craftsmen were resettled in Cusco.
ev.amr_h_chimor.ignore: Your own craft is just as good
ev.amr_h_pachacuti_death.title: Pachacuti has gone to the Sun
ev.amr_h_pachacuti_death.text: The great Pachacuti has died. His body will be preserved, and his mummy will go on "living" in his palace with his servants. Topa Inca Yupanqui has become Inca.
ev.amr_h_pachacuti_death.note: Pachacuti died around 1471. The mummies of Inca rulers were preserved, venerated and even carried to festivals; their palaces and lands stayed with their descendants.
ev.amr_h_huayna_capac.title: Huayna Capac
ev.amr_h_huayna_capac.text: Topa Inca has died. After disputes at court his son Huayna Capac has become Inca. He is touring the realm, and every road carries news of new censuses and new labours.
ev.amr_h_huayna_capac.note: Huayna Capac ruled from about 1493 to 1527/28. Under him the realm reached its greatest extent.
ev.amr_h_tomebamba.title: The court in the north
ev.amr_h_tomebamba.text: Huayna Capac has lived in the north for years, fighting rebellious tribes. Quito and Tomebamba have become almost a second capital: palaces, temples, storehouses, crowds of nobles from Cusco.
ev.amr_h_tomebamba.note: Huayna Capac spent much of his reign in the north, at Tomebamba (now Cuenca) and Quito. His son Atahualpa grew up at the northern court.
ev.amr_h_smallpox_an.title: A plague without an enemy
ev.amr_h_smallpox_an.text: A disease no one knew has come from the north: rash, fever, death within days. No one here has seen any strangers, yet the plague is already here. They say Huayna Capac himself has died, and after him his heir.
ev.amr_h_smallpox_an.note: An epidemic, probably smallpox, ran ahead of the Spaniards and around 1527–1528 killed Huayna Capac and his heir Ninan Cuyuchi. This led to a war over the throne.
ev.amr_h_smallpox_an.care.failure: You caught it and hovered between life and death for a long time.
ev.amr_h_smallpox_an.huaca: Bring gifts to the huacas and pray
ev.amr_h_smallpox_an.huaca.success: The plague passed your house by.
ev.amr_h_smallpox_an.huaca.failure: The disease came to you too.
ev.amr_h_civil_war.title: The brothers' war
ev.amr_h_civil_war.text: Huáscar rules in Cusco, Atahualpa in the north with his father's veterans. The brothers are fighting for the whole realm. The curacas must choose a side, and so must ordinary people.
ev.amr_h_civil_war.note: The civil war between Huáscar and Atahualpa (c. 1529–1532) devastated the realm. Atahualpa's generals took Cusco and dealt brutally with Huáscar's kin shortly before the Spaniards arrived.
ev.amr_h_civil_war.hide.failure: The war came anyway: fields trampled, stores seized.
ev.amr_h_cajamarca.title: The Inca a captive
ev.amr_h_cajamarca.text: Impossible news: a handful of bearded strangers on huge animals seized Atahualpa at Cajamarca in the middle of his army. For the Inca's freedom they demand a room filled with gold. Gold from the temples is being carried along every road.
ev.amr_h_cajamarca.note: On 16 November 1532 Francisco Pizarro's band captured Atahualpa at Cajamarca. A vast ransom was gathered, but in July 1533 the Spaniards executed the Inca.
ev.amr_h_cajamarca.give: Give your gold for the ransom
ev.amr_h_spanish_cusco.title: Spaniards in Cusco
ev.amr_h_spanish_cusco.text: The strangers have entered the capital. They are tearing the gold sheets from the walls of Coricancha, breaking into the palaces of the dead Incas and sharing out the nobles' houses among themselves. They have made young Manco the new Inca.
ev.amr_h_spanish_cusco.note: The Spaniards entered Cusco on 15 November 1533 and plundered its temples. Manco Inca Yupanqui was at first their ally and a puppet ruler.
ev.amr_h_spanish_cusco.hide: Leave the city for your kin
ev.amr_h_ruminahui.title: Quito in flames
ev.amr_h_ruminahui.text: The general Rumiñahui will not give Quito to the Spaniards. He has ordered the treasures carried away and the city burned so the strangers get nothing. The people are ordered to leave.
ev.amr_h_ruminahui.note: In 1534 Rumiñahui burned Quito before Sebastián de Belalcázar's force arrived. The Spaniards refounded the city that same year. Rumiñahui's treasure was never found.
ev.amr_h_ruminahui.follow.success: You survived in the mountains and later quietly came back.
ev.amr_h_ruminahui.follow.failure: The army was routed and you barely escaped.
ev.amr_h_ruminahui.stay: Stay and wait for the Spaniards
ev.amr_h_manco.title: Manco's rebellion
ev.amr_h_manco.text: Manco Inca has escaped from the Spaniards and raised an army. A huge host has surrounded Cusco, and burning arrows are falling on the thatched roofs. The Spaniards are holed up in a few buildings by the square.
ev.amr_h_manco.note: In 1536 Manco Inca besieged Cusco for almost a year. The siege failed, and Manco withdrew to the mountain region of Vilcabamba, where the Incas held out until 1572.
ev.amr_h_manco.join.success: You fought through the siege and went to the mountains with Manco alive.
ev.amr_h_manco.join.failure: You fell in the battle for the fortress of Sacsayhuaman.
ev.amr_h_manco.wait: Take shelter and wait it out
ev.amr_h_potosi.title: The silver mountain
ev.amr_h_potosi.text: Far to the south a mountain full of silver has been found. The Spaniards demand men from the communities to work the mines; they call it mit'a, but this work shares nothing with the old mit'a except the name.
ev.amr_h_potosi.note: The silver of Potosí was discovered in 1545. Later the Spaniards turned the Inca labour duty into forced labour in the mines, which cost a great many lives.
ev.amr_h_potosi.pay: Buy yourself out with cloth and llamas
